meta.title: Plant Doctor knowledge base - common indoor plant problems
meta.author: E. Sioras (34792945)

sources.UCIPM: D. R. Pittenger and D. R. Hodel, 'Houseplant Problems', UC IPM Pest Notes, Publication 74172, Univ. of California ANR, Aug. 2020.
sources.ISU: A. Steil, 'Diagnosing Houseplant Problems from Improper Environmental Conditions', Iowa State Univ. Extension and Outreach, rev. Jan. 2024.
sources.UMD: University of Maryland Extension, 'Indoor Plant Problems - Nonliving' and 'Indoor Plant Insects', 2023-2025.

plant_type.text: What kind of plant is it?

options.succulent: Succulent or cactus (aloe, jade, snake plant...)
options.tropical_foliage: Tropical foliage plant (pothos, monstera, peace lily, ficus, philodendron...)

plant_type.help: Different plant groups tolerate water, light and humidity differently.

leaf_yellowing.text: Are any leaves turning yellow? If so, where?
leaf_yellowing.help: Older-leaf yellowing usually points to roots, watering or nitrogen; new-leaf yellowing to waterlogging or micronutrients.

leaf_browning.text: Is there any browning on the leaves? Pick the best match.

options.crispy_tips_edges: Dry, crispy brown tips or edges
options.scorched_patches: Bleached, faded or scorched patches on the most exposed leaves
options.soft_dark_spots: Soft, dark or water-soaked spots or blotches

wilting.text: Is the plant wilting or drooping?

options.yes: Yes, more than the occasional old leaf

growth.text: How would you describe recent growth?

options.leggy: Leggy - long, stretched, spindly stems leaning toward light
options.stunted: Slow or stunted - very little new growth, small leaves

speckled_leaves.text: Do the leaves have fine yellow speckling or a dull, stippled / bronzed look?
speckled_leaves.help: Hold a leaf up to the light; tiny pale dots all over the surface are 'stippling'.

soil_moisture.text: Push a finger 2-3 cm into the potting mix. How does it feel?

options.soggy: Soggy / wet, even days after watering
options.dry_hard: Bone dry, hard or pulling away from the pot

watering_frequency.text: How often do you water compared with the plant's usual needs?

options.often: Often - on a schedule or whenever I think of it, even if still moist
options.regular: When the top of the mix has dried out
options.infrequent: Rarely - I often forget or go away

options.good: Yes - it has holes and does not sit in water
options.poor: No - no drainage hole, or it sits in a saucer / decorative pot of water

light_level.text: Where does the plant sit, light-wise?

options.low: Low light - away from windows, dim room or corner
options.medium: Medium - a few metres from a window
options.bright_indirect: Bright, indirect light near a window
options.direct_sun: Direct sun for several hours (on a sunny sill or outdoors)

recent_move.text: Has the plant been moved or had a big change in conditions in the last few weeks?

options.to_brighter: Moved somewhere much brighter / into sun
options.cold_transport: Just bought / carried home in cold weather

temperature.text: Is the plant near a temperature extreme?

options.cold_draft: Near a cold draught - door, window glass in winter, air-con outlet
options.heater_vent: Near a heater or hot-air vent

humidity.text: How humid is the air around the plant?

options.dry: Dry - heating or air-con running, or a dry climate
options.humid: Humid - bathroom, kitchen, terrarium or misted often

options.often: Often / more than the label says
options.normal: As the label suggests during the growing season

soil_crust.text: Is there a white or yellowish crust on the soil surface or pot rim?

water_dries_fast.text: Does the mix dry out within a day or two of a thorough watering, or does water run straight through?

stem_base.text: Feel the base of the stems where they enter the soil. Are they firm?

roots.text: If you can, gently slide the plant out of its pot. What do the roots look like?

options.mushy_brown: Brown or black, soft, mushy; outer layer slips off
options.circling_crowded: A dense mat circling the pot / growing out of the holes

rot_smell.text: Does the potting mix or root area smell sour or rotten?

pests_seen.text: Have you noticed any insects, webbing, white fluff, bumps or sticky residue on the plant?

webbing.text: Is there fine, silky webbing - especially at leaf joints or the undersides of leaves?

cottony_white.text: Are there white, cottony or waxy clumps in leaf joints or along stems?

bumps_on_stems.text: Are there small, immobile brown or tan bumps on stems or along leaf veins that can be scraped off?

clustered_insects.text: Are there clusters of small soft-bodied insects (green, black or pink) on new shoots or buds?

sticky_leaves.text: Are leaves (or the surface below the plant) sticky or shiny, or is there black sooty mould?

curled_new_growth.text: Are new leaves curled, twisted or distorted?

small_flies.text: Are there tiny dark flies hovering around the soil or nearby windows?

white_powder.text: Is there a white to grey powdery coating on leaves or stems that wipes off with a finger?

overwatering.name: Overwatering / waterlogged potting mix
overwatering.explanation: Roots sitting in saturated mix are starved of oxygen, so they cannot take up water and nutrients. Older leaves yellow and drop, and the plant may wilt even though the soil is wet.
actions: Stop watering until the top 2-5 cm of mix has dried out; then water only when it is dry.
Make sure the pot has drainage holes and empty any saucer or cover pot after watering.
If the mix stays wet for more than a week, repot into fresh, free-draining mix in a pot that is not oversized.
Check the roots for rot (brown, mushy roots).

underwatering.name: Underwatering / drought stress
underwatering.explanation: The root ball has dried out, so the plant cannot replace water lost through its leaves. Leaves droop, then become dry and crispy from the edges.
actions: Soak the pot thoroughly until water runs from the drainage holes; if the mix has shrunk from the pot, stand it in a bucket of water for 30 minutes.
Then water whenever the top few centimetres of mix are dry rather than on a fixed schedule.
Consider a self-watering pot or a reminder if you often forget.

root_rot.name: Root rot (water-mould fungi such as Pythium / Phytophthora)
root_rot.explanation: Persistently wet mix has allowed root-rotting organisms to destroy part of the root system. Damaged roots cannot supply water, so the plant wilts, yellows and stunts, and the base of the stems may soften.
actions: Remove the plant from its pot and wash or shake off the old mix.
Cut away all brown, mushy roots with clean, disinfected scissors.
Repot in fresh, well-drained potting mix in a clean pot with drainage holes; water sparingly afterwards.
If most roots or the stem base are rotten, take healthy cuttings and discard the rest of the plant.

insufficient_light.name: Insufficient light
insufficient_light.explanation: Without enough light the plant cannot photosynthesise enough to support its leaves. Stems stretch toward the light (leggy growth), new leaves are small, and older leaves yellow and drop.
actions: Move the plant to a brighter spot with bright, indirect light (closer to a window).
Acclimatise gradually over 1-2 weeks to avoid scorch, or add a grow light.
Water less while light is low, as the mix will dry more slowly.
Prune leggy stems back; new growth will be more compact.

excess_light.name: Sun scorch / too much direct light
excess_light.explanation: Strong direct sun, or a sudden move into brighter light, has damaged leaf tissue. Exposed leaves develop bleached, faded or brown scorched patches. Scorch damage is permanent.
actions: Move the plant out of direct midday sun, or filter the light with a sheer curtain.
When moving plants to brighter spots, acclimatise them gradually over several weeks.
Trim badly damaged leaves for appearance; new leaves will grow normally.

low_humidity.name: Low humidity
low_humidity.explanation: Dry air - from heating, air-conditioning or a dry climate - pulls water from leaves faster than the plant can replace it. Humidity-loving plants show crispy brown tips and edges first.
actions: Raise humidity: group plants together, use a pebble tray or a humidifier.
Move the plant away from heaters, vents and air-conditioner outlets.
Trimming brown tips is cosmetic only - browning returns unless humidity improves.
If tips keep browning, also consider your water source (chlorine / fluoride affects calathea, dracaena and spider plants).

fertiliser_burn.name: Fertiliser / salt build-up
fertiliser_burn.explanation: Excess fertiliser or minerals from tap water have accumulated in the mix. High salt levels damage roots and cause brown, burnt leaf tips and margins; a white crust often forms on the soil surface.
actions: Flush the pot: slowly run water through the mix equal to about 2-3 times the pot's volume, letting it drain.
Scrape off any crusted top layer of mix, or repot in fresh mix if heavily affected.
Reduce fertiliser to the label rate (or half) and only feed during active growth.

nutrient_deficiency.name: Nutrient deficiency (usually nitrogen)
nutrient_deficiency.explanation: The plant has used up the nutrients in its potting mix. Nitrogen is mobile, so the plant moves it to new growth and the older, lower leaves turn pale yellow-green; growth slows.
actions: Feed with a balanced liquid houseplant fertiliser at the label rate during spring and summer.
Repot plants that have been in the same mix for more than 2 years.
Do not over-correct - too much fertiliser causes salt burn.

cold_draft_stress.name: Cold / draught stress
cold_draft_stress.explanation: Exposure to cold draughts, cold window glass or chilly transport has chilled the tissues of a tropical plant. This commonly causes sudden leaf drop, yellowing, or dark water-soaked patches.
actions: Move the plant away from doors, cold window glass and air-conditioner outlets.
Keep tropical plants above about 13-15 C, and protect them with a bag or box when transporting in cold weather.
Remove damaged leaves and avoid overwatering while the plant recovers.

pot_bound.name: Pot-bound (root-bound) plant
pot_bound.explanation: Roots have filled the pot, leaving little mix to hold water and nutrients. The plant dries out quickly, growth stalls and leaf tips may brown.
actions: Repot into a container one size (2-5 cm) larger with fresh potting mix.
Gently tease out circling roots before repotting.
Water thoroughly after repotting.

spider_mites.name: Spider mites
spider_mites.explanation: Tiny sap-sucking mites feed on the undersides of leaves, leaving fine yellow speckling (stippling) and bronzing. Heavy infestations produce fine webbing. They thrive in warm, dry air.
actions: Isolate the plant from your other plants.
Wash leaves (especially the undersides) with a strong spray of water regularly; raise humidity.
Remove heavily infested leaves.
As a last resort, use insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, repeated weekly; discard plants with persistent infestations.

mealybugs.name: Mealybugs
mealybugs.explanation: Soft-bodied insects covered in white, cottony wax cluster in leaf joints and along stems. They suck sap, causing yellowing, stunting and sticky honeydew.
actions: Isolate the plant.
Wipe off mealybugs, or dab small colonies with a cotton bud dipped in 70% isopropyl alcohol (test on one leaf first).
Apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil for larger infestations, repeating every 7-10 days.
Discard heavily infested plants.

scale_insects.name: Scale insects
scale_insects.explanation: Immobile insects protected by a brown or waxy shell attach to stems and leaf veins and suck sap. They produce sticky honeydew that can grow black sooty mould, and cause yellowing and dieback.
actions: Isolate the plant.
Scrape off adult scale with a fingernail or soft brush; wipe leaves to remove crawlers and honeydew.
Apply horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, repeating to catch newly hatched crawlers.

fungus_gnats.name: Fungus gnats
fungus_gnats.explanation: Tiny dark flies breed in constantly moist potting mix. The adults are a nuisance; their larvae feed on fine roots, which can cause wilting and poor growth in seedlings and small plants.
actions: Let the top few centimetres of mix dry out between waterings - larvae need moist mix.
Empty saucers and remove standing water.
Use yellow sticky traps to catch adults.
Drench the mix with a Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis) product, repeated as directed.

aphids.name: Aphids
aphids.explanation: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects feed on tender new shoots and buds, causing curled or distorted new leaves and sticky honeydew.
actions: Hose or wash aphids off with water.
Remove and bag heavily infested shoots.
Apply insecticidal soap or horticultural oil if they return.

powdery_mildew.name: Powdery mildew
powdery_mildew.explanation: A fungal disease forming a white-grey powdery coating on leaves and stems. It is rarely fatal but unsightly, and is favoured by poor air circulation and low light.
actions: Remove the worst affected leaves.
Improve air circulation and move the plant into brighter light; keep it away from cold draughts.
Water early in the day and avoid wetting the foliage.

rules.note: Watering too often keeps the mix saturated.
No drainage hole or a saucer of water keeps the mix saturated.
Soggy mix days after watering indicates excess moisture.
Frequent watering in low light - the mix never gets a chance to dry.
Infrequent watering and a bone-dry root ball.
Bone-dry mix indicates a water deficit.
Brown, soft roots are the defining sign of root decay.
Soft stem bases indicate rot spreading from the roots / crown.
A sour or rotten odour accompanies rotting tissue.
Plant positioned in low light.
Stretching in medium light shows light is still limiting for this plant.
Sticky honeydew / sooty mould is excreted by sap-sucking insects.
White crust is mineral and fertiliser salt deposit.
Frequent fertilising leads to soluble-salt accumulation.
Yellowing with saturated mix is the classic overwatering pattern.
Wilting despite wet mix - waterlogged roots cannot take up water.
Saturated mix on its own is a likely cause of problems.
Succulents are especially prone to overwatering and crown rot.
Evidence against: the mix is dry.
Wilting with a dry root ball is usually underwatering.
Letting the plant dry out too long browns tips and edges.
A dry root ball on its own suggests underwatering.
Evidence against: the mix is wet.
Damaged roots in saturated mix - water-mould root rot.
Rotted roots cannot supply water, so the plant wilts.
Signs of root / crown decay.
Evidence against: roots are white and firm.
Once roots are rotting, root rot (not just wet mix) is the more specific diagnosis.
Leggy, stretched growth in poor light is the classic low-light symptom.
Spindly growth is typically caused by low light.
Inadequate light causes older leaves to yellow and drop.
A move from bright to dim light causes leaf drop (e.g. weeping fig).
Low light is a contributing stress.
Evidence against: the plant already has good light.
Poor light causes weak, slow growth.
Bleached / scorched patches on plants in direct sun.
Sunburn after a sudden move into brighter light.
Pale, bleached patches are typical of excess light.
Evidence against: the plant is in low light.
Low humidity is the most common cause of brown leaf tips.
Humidity-loving species brown at the tips first in dry air.
Hot, dry air from heaters dries leaf margins.
Brown tips are most often humidity-related.
Evidence against: the air is humid.
A dry root ball explains crispy tips better than air humidity.
Salt build-up explains crispy tips better than air humidity.
Browning tips and margins with salt build-up - fertiliser toxicity.
Evidence of excess soluble salts.
Evidence against: little fertiliser and no salt crust.
Excessive fertiliser or salts can cause leaf drop.
Yellow-green older leaves with no feeding - nitrogen deficiency.
Poor growth due to lack of nutrients.
General light-green / yellow foliage with no feeding.
Waterlogging produces the same yellowing; treat watering first.
Evidence against: the plant is fed often.
Insufficient light also causes yellow-green older leaves.
Cold draughts cause leaf drop in tropical plants.
Chilling injury produces dark, water-soaked spots.
Low temperatures cause yellowing and dropping leaves.
Cold exposure during transport causes leaf drop.
Temperature fluctuation from draughts is a stress factor.
Roots filling and circling the pot.
Mix dries very fast and growth stalls - roots have filled the pot.
Pot-bound plants dry out, browning leaf tips.
A pot-bound plant wilts soon after watering.
Evidence against: roots are not crowded.
Fast drying is explained by a full root ball, not neglect.
Stippling plus webbing is diagnostic of spider mites.
Fine webbing near growing points.
Speckled, bronzed leaves in dry air favour mites.
Speckled yellowing is a feeding sign of mites.
Cottony white wax in leaf joints is diagnostic of mealybugs.
Honeydew confirms a sap-feeding insect.
Honeydew can come from mealybugs.
Small immobile bumps on stems and veins are scale insects.
Sticky leaves and sooty mould accompany scale.
Honeydew can come from scale.
Small dark flies breeding in constantly wet mix.
Tiny dark flies around soil and windows.
Gnat larvae need moist mix; dry mix makes them less likely.
Clusters on new shoots with distorted leaves - aphids.
Soft-bodied insects clustered on new growth.
Curled leaves with honeydew suggest aphids.
Honeydew can come from aphids.
White-grey powder that wipes off is powdery mildew.
Low light favours powdery mildew.
Clumped cottony wax suggests mealybugs rather than a mildew film.
